subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Give the equation of reaction for the preparation of phenol from cumene.

mark_split.label: Acid hydrolysis to phenol and acetone
Why this is the industrial route

verification.note: Unit 16 (Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.108-112, from the shaded sub-box "ALCOHOLS, PHENOLS AND ETHERS" of printed chapter 12 ("12. ORGANIC CHEMISTRY", a container of four unnumbered sub-boxes each restarting at 1). The book prints this question on book p.109 as Short Answer 1. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK NAMING ERROR, corrected on this card (book p.109, SAQ 1): the printed scheme labels the intermediate "cumene peroxide". It is cumene HYDROperoxide — its group is –O–O–H, not the R–O–O–R of a true peroxide. The card writes cumene hydroperoxide and records the book's label. BOOK SLOPPINESS: the printed arrow for the second stage carries "H⁺ / H₂O", which reads as though water were a reactant. It is not: the rearrangement is acid catalysed and the balanced equation C₉H₁₂O₂ → C₆H₆O + C₃H₆O needs no water at all (C 9=9, H 12=12, O 2=2). Dilute H₂SO₄ is the catalyst and the medium; the card says so. BALANCE CHECKED: C₆H₅CH(CH₃)₂ + O₂ → C₆H₅C(CH₃)₂OOH balances as C₉H₁₂ + O₂ = C₉H₁₂O₂. BOOK GAP: the printed answer gives no temperature; air oxidation is carried out at about 373 K. TREND AND EXCEPTION: the card states that oxidation happens at the tertiary benzylic C–H because it is the weakest C–H in the molecule, and names the exception on the same card — with a strong oxidising agent such as KMnO₄ any alkyl side chain carrying a benzylic hydrogen is oxidised right down to –COOH, so toluene gives benzoic acid rather than a hydroperoxide, and this mild route works only with the branched isopropyl side chain.

steps.label: What cumene is
lines: Its side chain carries one hydrogen on a
carbon that holds the ring and two methyl
groups, so that C–H is a tertiary benzylic
This is the C–H that is oxidised.
steps.why: Naming the tertiary benzylic hydrogen is the reason the whole route works: it is the weakest C–H bond in the molecule, so air alone can remove it. Every later step follows from where that first oxygen goes.
common_mistakes: Writing cumene as propylbenzene. The side chain is branched, so it is isopropylbenzene.
Saying the ring is oxidised. The ring is untouched throughout; only the side chain reacts.
steps.memory_tip: Cumene is a benzene ring with an isopropyl group, and the single hydrogen on that branch carbon is the one that reacts.
steps.margin_note: Draw or write the structure once. The examiner needs to see that you know which hydrogen is oxidised.

steps.label: Air oxidation to cumene hydroperoxide
lines: Cumene is oxidised by air at about 373 K.
steps.why: An oxygen molecule adds at the tertiary benzylic carbon, giving the –O–O–H group. The equation balances as it stands, C₉H₁₂ plus O₂ giving C₉H₁₂O₂, so nothing else is formed at this stage. The exception worth knowing is that a stronger oxidising agent such as KMnO₄ does not stop here at all; it oxidises an alkyl side chain right down to –COOH, which is why toluene gives benzoic acid and not a hydroperoxide.
common_mistakes: Calling the product cumene peroxide, as the book does. A peroxide is R–O–O–R; this is R–O–O–H, a hydroperoxide.
Adding water to this step. Air is the only other reactant and the equation balances without water.
steps.memory_tip: Air puts O₂ straight onto the branch carbon, giving –O–O–H, the hydroperoxide.
steps.margin_note: Write air or O₂ above the arrow. The reagent is the cheap part of this process and the examiner looks for it.

steps.label: Acid hydrolysis to phenol and acetone
lines: The hydroperoxide is treated with dilute
H₂SO₄. The chain rearranges and breaks.
Phenol and acetone are formed together.
steps.why: The acid is a catalyst, not a reactant: the equation C₉H₁₂O₂ giving C₆H₆O plus C₃H₆O balances with no water on either side. The ring migrates from carbon to oxygen and the C–C bond then breaks, which is how one molecule gives two.
common_mistakes: Putting H₂O on the left of this equation. Water is the medium; the balanced equation needs none.
Giving propanal as the second product. The carbon that breaks away carries two methyl groups, so the product is acetone.
steps.memory_tip: One hydroperoxide splits into two useful products: phenol from the ring side, acetone from the branch side.
steps.margin_note: Name acetone in words as well as in the formula. It is half of what this step produces.

steps.label: Why this is the industrial route
lines: Phenol is separated from acetone by
Both products are wanted, and the only
This is the main industrial method of
steps.why: Other routes to phenol consume an expensive reagent and give a by-product with no use, so the reason this method is used on a large scale is that its by-product is itself a saleable chemical and its oxidant is free.
common_mistakes: Calling acetone a waste product. Acetone is sold as well, and that is the point of the route.
Writing that the two products are separated by filtration. Both are liquids, so they are separated by distillation.
steps.memory_tip: Air in, two useful liquids out. That is why industry uses cumene.
steps.margin_note: One sentence on why the route is used industrially finishes the answer. Do not stop at the last equation.

insider_note: The intermediate is cumene HYDROperoxide, –O–O–H, although the book labels it cumene peroxide. Name it correctly, and do not write water on the left of the second equation — the acid is a catalyst and the equation balances without it.
